Systemic means relating to, embedded in, or affecting an entire system as a whole — not just one isolated part of it.

When you call something systemic, you're saying: this isn't a surface-level or localized thing. It runs deep. It is woven into the structure of the whole system itself.

Think of a system as any organized, interconnected whole — a human body, a company, a government, a financial network, a society. Something systemic doesn't just touch one corner of that system. It exists throughout it, or it comes from within its very structure.
A Simple Image to Lock It In

Imagine a large building. If one room has a broken window, that's an isolated problem. But if the entire foundation is cracked, that's a systemic problem — it lives in the structure of the building itself, and no matter how many windows you fix, the building is still in danger.

That's the essence of systemic: the problem (or quality) is in the system, not just in one part of it.

1. Medicine and Biology

In medicine, systemic means affecting the whole body, as opposed to one localized area.

  • A systemic infection has spread through the bloodstream and is affecting the whole body — not just, say, a wound on the skin.
  • A systemic disease like lupus attacks multiple organs and systems in the body simultaneously.
  • Doctors distinguish between a local reaction (redness on your arm after a vaccine) and a systemic reaction (fever, fatigue, chills — your whole body responding).

In this context, systemic is almost always neutral or descriptive — it just tells you the scope of something.

2. Society, Politics, and Institutions

This is probably where you'll hear systemic most often today.

  • Systemic racism doesn't just mean individual people holding racist beliefs. It means racism that is built into the structures and policies of institutions — laws, hiring practices, school funding formulas, policing policies — so that even without any one person intending harm, the system itself produces unequal outcomes. The racism is in the system, not just in individual hearts.
  • Systemic corruption in a government means corruption isn't just present in a few bad officials — it is embedded in how the institution operates. It's the norm, not the exception.
  • Systemic inequality in education means the inequality isn't random or occasional — it arises from the way the educational system is structured.

The key implication when used this way: it's not an accident, and you can't fix it by just replacing a few individuals. You have to change the system.

3. Finance and Economics

  • Systemic risk refers to a risk that threatens the entire financial system — not just one company. This is why the 2008 financial crisis was so alarming. Large banks were so deeply interconnected that the collapse of one threatened to bring down the whole network. That interconnected vulnerability was the systemic risk.
  • A systemically important bank is one so deeply embedded in the financial system that if it fails, it drags the entire system with it.

4. Agriculture and Ecology

  • A systemic pesticide or herbicide is one that gets absorbed into the plant's tissues and circulates throughout the entire plant — rather than just coating the surface. It works from the inside out, through the plant's whole system.
The Most Important Distinction: Systemic vs. Systematic

These two words look similar but mean very different things, and confusing them is one of the most common mistakes.

SystematicDone in an organized, planned, step-by-step way.
SystemicRelating to or embedded in a whole system.
  • "She took a systematic approach to learning English." — She was organized and methodical. She had a plan and followed it step by step.
  • "The school has a systemic problem with underfunding." — The problem isn't random or occasional. It runs throughout the structure of how the school operates.

A systematic problem means a problem that keeps happening in a regular pattern (maybe because there's no proper plan to handle it).

A systemic problem means a problem that is embedded in the system itself.

You can have both at once: "The country has a systemic healthcare crisis, and doctors are systematically undertrained." — The crisis is structural and widespread (systemic); and the undertraining happens in a consistent, patterned way across all medical schools (systematic).

When you call something systemic, you're often (though not always) implying two things:

  1. Scale — it is widespread, affecting the whole, not just a part.
  2. Origin — it comes from within the structure of the system, not from outside it or from a single bad actor.

This is why systemic carries weight. If someone says "we have a few bad employees," that's a personnel problem. If someone says "we have systemic problems in our company culture," they mean: the problem isn't a few individuals — it's in how the company is organized, incentivized, and run. Fixing it requires changing the system itself.
Quick Examples to See It in Action

• "The patient's symptoms worsened when the infection became systemic." — It spread throughout the whole body.
  • "Poverty in that region is systemic — it has persisted for generations because the economic structures keep people trapped." — It's not bad luck; it's structural.
  • "The bank was considered a systemic risk to the economy." — Its failure could bring down the whole financial system.
  • "The company discovered systemic flaws in its quality control." — Not one-off mistakes, but problems embedded in how the whole process works.
  • "The herbicide is systemic, so it kills the weed roots and all." — It spreads through the whole plant's system.

Systemic describes something that is not isolated or surface-level, but rather is embedded in, spread throughout, or characteristic of an entire system as a whole — and often implies that fixing it requires changing the system, not just patching one part.
